cells.tense: You are carrying what you've been taught into rooms where it can be used.
cells.ask: Tell someone younger than you one thing you learned the hard way, in plain words, and let them try it their own way. Ten minutes. Then watch what they do with it and don't correct them.
cells.core:
You're handing something on and it keeps changing in your hands. Not reciting rules that came down to you — the words come out different each time, shaped to who's in front of you, and it's still the same thing underneath. People take it and make their own use of it. That's what keeps it alive.

You're doing this while holding a lot that hasn't been sorted yet: what to pass on, what to drop, what was only ever meant for one season. The balance here isn't standing still between old and new. It's the ongoing adjustment — sensing when to say it as you got it and when to say it as you now understand it. Keep checking where the line lands. That checking is the work, and a good line today doesn't retire it.
cells.sheetLine: You keep what was given alive by giving it away differently.

cells.tense: You're bracing for a version of this that hasn't happened yet, and it's making everything rigid.
cells.ask: Pick one way you do things — one habit, one rule — and skip it deliberately for a day. Not because it's wrong. Just to see what was holding it up.
cells.core:
You're guarding the shape of something that hasn't arrived yet — the right way to do it, the way you learned, and you're enforcing that before anyone has asked you to. The instructions got loud. The room got small. Somewhere a rule that started as a way to keep things good turned into a way to keep things still.

This piece is about passing on what people gave you, and right now it's doing the opposite. It demands the same response from whoever is in front of you, at the same volume, before they get to find their own foothold. The old forms aren't the enemy. Being unable to set one down is. Watch for the rule that stops holding on its own — when it goes, the space opens.

cells.tense: You're standing at a door that's already closed behind you, and you've been out here so long you've stopped expecting to go back in.
cells.ask: Ask someone you trust how they do one thing you've been figuring out alone. Ask it as a real question, not a test. Then use any part of the answer that fits.
cells.core:
You've been building it alone. No shared set of ways, no line you can trace back — each problem solved from scratch, each insight yours to hold. There's real intelligence in this, and real weight. Nobody handed you a form, and it isn't clear one exists.

Ideas aren't the shortage. The shortage is the sense that anyone came before you, that there's ground under the ground. Without it, whatever you learn stays locked to the particular case — it can't travel, and it can't be handed on. So the next move is finding the pattern underneath: how a thing works once you strip the details away. That's what turns one solved problem into something another person can use. The pattern points back to a place you can stand in.

cells.tense: You're already standing where people are learning from you, and you're calling it something else.
cells.ask: Name one thing you do that someone else picked up from watching you. Say it out loud, to yourself or to them. No modesty move, no 'I was just doing my job'.
cells.core:
People take things from you. A phrase you repeat, a way of deciding, how you answer a hard question — someone has already copied it, changed it a little, made it their own. It's happening in how you're read, not just in what you say.

None of that is a statement about your worth, and it doesn't prove anything about your past. It's just what's happening: influence running without anyone claiming it, and the one person who could say 'that came from me' acting like it arrived on its own. You don't have to do more to deserve the credit. You only have to stop calling it the situation. The balance you're after is nothing more than taking hold of what's already moving. It was yours before you signed it.

attempts.check: The record calls this seat 'pure possibility before differentiation', which is an abstract claim about their state, not something observable; a reader could reasonably say they simply haven't decided anything yet about what they hand on. The ask in each cell survives being wrong because it is a small, reversible act grounded in what is visible — someone they learned from, something they repeat — and teaches them something regardless of my read. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you're the teacher already' said as a verdict rather than an offer; it's cut where it would flatter the writer and kept only as present-tense evidence for the person to accept or reject.
